# Results — Study 59 (Downhill): riding the yield curve (the term premium), 2003–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly total returns of **IEF** (7–10y
Treasuries), **SHY** (1–3y) and **BIL** (cash/T-bills), Yahoo, 2003–2026. Inputs fingerprint
`e3c760f99f78`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `FRAGILE` · "Is the duration risk worth it"? `NOT SUPPORTED`

The term premium is `REAL`: holding intermediate Treasuries (IEF) instead of cash (BIL) earned an excess
of **+2.2%/yr** over 2003–2026 — longer bonds do pay more than bills on average. But that return is
**poorly compensated risk**, so `FRAGILE` and `NOT SUPPORTED`: the excess earns a Sharpe of just
**0.32 (t 1.4)**, and *holding cash had a Sharpe of 1.82* while 1–3y bonds had **1.13** — three-to-five
times better risk-adjusted than extending to 7–10y. Stretching for the term premium also bought a
**−23% drawdown** in the 2022 bond crash. The premium exists; reaching for it with duration was a bad
trade on a risk-adjusted basis.

## Data stamp

- **Panel**: IEF (7–10y) / SHY (1–3y) / BIL (cash), monthly total return, 2003–2026, fingerprint
  `e3c760f99f78`

## More duration bought more return — and far more risk

| | CAGR | Sharpe | vol | max-DD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| IEF (7–10y) | +3.3% | **0.52** | 6.7% | **−23%** |
| SHY (1–3y) | +1.9% | **1.13** | 1.6% | −5% |
| BIL (cash) | +1.4% | **1.82** | 0.7% | −0% |

The return ladder is monotone in duration — longer bonds earned more — but so is the *risk* ladder, and
much more steeply: the Sharpe **falls** as you extend, from 1.82 (cash) to 0.52 (7–10y). You were paid
for duration, just not nearly enough.

## The term premium, isolated

| IEF − BIL (the term premium / roll-down) | value |
|---|---|
| mean | **+2.2%/yr** |
| Sharpe | **0.32** |
| t-stat | 1.4 |
| hit rate | 52% |

A positive but weakly significant excess (t 1.4), winning barely half the months, at a Sharpe a fraction
of cash's. The 2003–2026 window includes the four-decade bond bull *and* its violent 2022 reversal —
which is exactly the duration risk the premium is supposed to compensate, and didn't, well.

## Why riding the curve disappointed

1. **Duration risk is convex and lumpy.** Most years the roll-down drips in quietly; then 2022 takes
   −17% in a single year. A Sharpe-blind investor sees the average; a risk-aware one sees the tail.
2. **The premium has compressed.** Decades of falling rates and QE pushed term premia toward (even
   below) zero; the realised excess leaned on capital gains from falling yields, not a stable carry.
3. **Short is efficient.** Bills and 1–3y notes captured most of the safe yield with a fraction of the
   risk — the efficient place on the curve for a cautious investor.

## The honest takeaway

The term premium is `REAL` — longer Treasuries beat cash by ~2%/yr — but `FRAGILE` and `NOT SUPPORTED`
as a trade: its Sharpe (0.32) is dwarfed by simply holding bills (1.82), and stretching for it bought a
−23% drawdown in 2022. Riding the curve earns extra return for extra risk that, historically, wasn't
worth taking. A real premium that the risk-adjusted numbers tell you to leave on the table.
